source_user: Explain how continuous batching interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: Assuming decoder inference with requests of unequal output lengths, continuous batching changes the active set at decode iteration boundaries: completed requests release their slots and queued requests can be admitted. This mechanism reduces idle work from length skew and can raise useful throughput, but admission and KV-cache allocation add scheduling and memory overhead. Latency is workload-dependent: queueing may increase time to first token or tail latency even when aggregate tokens/s improves. A boundary condition is available KV-cache capacity and scheduler policy; under low load, homogeneous lengths, or memory pressure, there may be little gain or even regressions. Compare a matched static baseline using the same arrivals, model, limits, and output lengths, and measure TTFT, inter-token latency, queue time, p95/p99, goodput, throughput, active-set occupancy, KV memory, evictions, and failures.
risks: Aggregate throughput can conceal queueing, starvation, or tail-latency regressions.
An undefined baseline may differ in padding, packing, admission, or failure policy.
evidence_required: Matched policy and workload definitions, iteration-level admission/retirement traces, request-level latency distributions, throughput/goodput, KV-memory telemetry, and error or eviction logs.

source_user: Explain how continuous batching interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: In autoregressive serving, continuous batching retires finished sequences and admits waiting ones at iteration boundaries, so a short request need not leave a slot idle until the longest request finishes. Reusing that active slot can improve device utilization and throughput under length skew. It does not guarantee lower latency: admission queueing, synchronization, and larger concurrent KV caches can raise TTFT, inter-token latency, or p99 latency. The boundary is the serving regime—at low concurrency or with equal lengths, slot reuse may provide little benefit, while near KV-memory capacity it can cause deferral, paging, rejection, or OOM. Evaluate identical request arrivals, length distribution, model/runtime, and resource limits; report queue time, TTFT, inter-token and tail latency, goodput, tokens/s, memory, cache events, and failures.
risks: Higher utilization may trade against fairness and request-level latency.
Memory-related admissions or failures can change the effective workload.
evidence_required: Explicit baseline semantics, controlled load/length sweeps, active-batch traces, request-level latency percentiles, throughput and goodput, memory headroom, and failure accounting.

source_user: Give a measurement plan for validating whether continuous batching helps a serving workload. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: Define a matched comparison between continuous batching and the chosen static or non-continuous baseline. Hold model weights, precision, hardware, runtime, prompt/output-length distributions, arrival trace, concurrency limit, sampling settings, and correctness criteria constant; state whether limits are hard caps. Sweep offered load and length skew, warm up, randomize run order, and repeat enough times to report uncertainty. Instrument iteration-level admissions/retirements and active batch size, then measure TTFT, inter-token latency, queue/service time, p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, goodput, utilization, KV-cache bytes, evictions, OOMs, timeouts, and rejected requests. The mechanism being tested is replacement of completed requests at iteration boundaries; the boundary is that gains may disappear when load is low or KV memory is saturated. Check output correctness and compare confidence intervals, not just mean tokens/s.
risks: Different admission or failure policies can make the compared workloads non-equivalent.
Averages and utilization can mask p99 latency, fairness, and correctness regressions.
evidence_required: Versioned configuration manifests, replayable arrival traces, repeated randomized runs, scheduler/KV telemetry, request-level metrics, correctness checks, and confidence intervals.

source_user: Give a measurement plan for validating whether continuous batching helps a serving workload. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: First specify the baseline (for example, fixed membership until completion), workload arrival process, prompt and generated-token distributions, concurrency, hardware, model/runtime version, precision, and admission/failure policy. Run both systems with the same replayed requests, warm-up, randomized order, and repeated seeds or trials across low, medium, and saturated load plus several length-skew levels. Log every iteration's active membership, retirement and admission events, queue time, and KV allocation. Measure TTFT, inter-token latency, p50/p95/p99 end-to-end latency, completed requests, goodput, tokens/s, device utilization, peak KV memory, paging/evictions, rejection, timeout, and OOM rates. The mechanism is slot replacement when a request completes; a boundary condition is scheduler synchronization or KV capacity, which can negate gains. Verify response correctness and report uncertainty and per-request distributions.
risks: Changing load generation or completion/failure handling biases throughput comparisons.
Cache paging and scheduler overhead may shift the bottleneck rather than improve service.
evidence_required: Matched workload replay, configuration and version records, iteration traces, KV-memory events, latency/queue distributions, goodput, failures, and repeated-run uncertainty.

source_user: Give a measurement plan for validating whether continuous batching helps a serving workload. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: Use a controlled A/B experiment with continuous batching and a precisely defined non-continuous baseline. Keep weights, tokenizer, hardware, precision, runtime, prompt mix, output limits, arrival timestamps, and resource quotas fixed; test several arrival rates, concurrency levels, and output-length distributions. After warm-up, repeat runs with randomized order. Capture admission and retirement timestamps, active batch size, queue delay, prefill/decode phases, KV-cache allocation, and device utilization. Report TTFT, inter-token latency, completion latency percentiles, throughput and goodput, utilization, peak memory, evictions, rejected/failed requests, and output correctness. The concrete mechanism is that a completed sequence's slot can be filled at an iteration boundary. The boundary condition is that safe admission may be blocked by KV-cache headroom or scheduler constraints, so continuous batching can worsen tails or failure rate despite higher occupancy. Include confidence intervals and per-request results.
risks: A single offered-load point cannot establish a general performance claim.
Occupancy gains may be accompanied by worse fairness, p99 latency, or reliability.
evidence_required: A/B manifests, fixed request traces, load and length matrix, scheduler/cache traces, request-level latency and queue metrics, correctness results, and uncertainty estimates.

source_user: What assumptions must be stated before making a performance claim about continuous batching? Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: State the serving phase (autoregressive decode versus prefill), model and runtime versions, hardware, precision, scheduler policy, maximum concurrency, KV-cache allocation/paging behavior, arrival process, prompt and output-length distributions, and the exact baseline. Define whether latency means TTFT, inter-token, or end-to-end latency, and whether throughput means generated tokens/s, completed requests/s, or goodput after failures. The mechanism is dynamic active-set replacement at iteration boundaries, which can reduce idle slots from length skew. A boundary condition is available KV memory and admission policy: if new requests cannot be safely admitted, or if load is low and lengths are homogeneous, the benefit may vanish or reverse. Claims require matched workloads, correctness checks, request-level latency and tail metrics, memory and failure measurements, and repeated trials; do not infer universal gains from utilization alone.
risks: Ambiguous metric definitions can make an apparent improvement incomparable.
Ignoring rejected, paged, or failed requests can inflate reported throughput.
evidence_required: Baseline and policy specification, workload/configuration manifest, request-level telemetry, KV-memory and scheduler events, correctness checks, and repeated measurements across load.

source_user: What assumptions must be stated before making a performance claim about continuous batching? Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: Before claiming better performance, specify what implementation is being compared, whether both systems use the same request mix and admission limits, and whether the measurement covers prefill, decode, or both. Also state hardware, model/precision, runtime and kernel versions, batch/concurrency policy, arrival rate, prompt/output lengths, memory budget, and definitions for throughput, goodput, TTFT, inter-token latency, and tail latency. Continuous batching works by retiring completed sequences and admitting queued work at iteration boundaries; its boundary is that scheduler synchronization, shape/packing rules, or KV-cache capacity can limit replacement and create queueing, paging, or rejection. Measure matched request-level outcomes, memory, utilization, and errors across load and length conditions with repeats and uncertainty. A tokens/s increase alone is insufficient evidence of a user-visible improvement.
risks: An unfair baseline or changed admission cap can confound the result.
Aggregate metrics may hide long-request starvation or tail degradation.
evidence_required: Explicit comparison policy, versioned environment and workload manifests, admission traces, request-level latency distributions, memory/cache telemetry, failure counts, and repeated load sweeps.

source_user: What assumptions must be stated before making a performance claim about continuous batching? Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: A defensible claim must identify the baseline's batching and admission semantics, workload arrival and length distributions, model, runtime, hardware, precision, scheduler, concurrency/resource limits, and cache-management policy. Define the service objectives and units: TTFT/inter-token/end-to-end latency, requests/s or tokens/s, goodput, and p95/p99. The mechanism is dynamic membership: completed requests are retired at an iteration boundary and queued requests may use the next active slot. The boundary is workload and capacity dependent; with low offered load, little length variation, or insufficient KV memory, replacement may not improve throughput and can increase queueing or failures. Use a matched replay, verify outputs, instrument active membership and cache events, measure request-level performance and reliability, and report repeated-run uncertainty rather than extrapolating from utilization.
risks: Performance conclusions can be invalid if decode and prefill are mixed without phase-specific metrics.
Memory pressure can alter admissions and invalidate equal-work assumptions.
evidence_required: Phase-specific benchmark definition, matched traces, scheduler and KV events, correctness validation, request-level tails, goodput, failure/rejection logs, and uncertainty across load.

source_user: What assumptions must be stated before making a performance claim about continuous batching? Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: State the exact continuous-batching and baseline algorithms, when membership changes, model/runtime/hardware/precision, prompt and output-token distributions, arrival process, concurrency and memory limits, scheduler fairness, and cache paging/eviction behavior. Define whether the claim concerns latency, throughput, utilization, cost, or goodput and give units plus percentile conventions. Mechanistically, retirement of finished requests at iteration boundaries permits queued requests to reuse subsequent decode capacity. The boundary is the admission decision: KV-cache headroom, packing constraints, synchronization, or queue policy may prevent immediate replacement and can worsen p99 or reliability. Validate with the same request trace and correctness criterion, load and length sweeps, repeated randomized trials, and telemetry for queueing, active-set changes, prefill/decode time, memory, evictions, timeouts, and OOMs. Treat any unmeasured platform-specific behavior as unknown.
risks: Unspecified scheduler fairness can turn utilization gains into unacceptable tail or starvation behavior.
Platform-specific packing and cache behavior cannot be assumed without evidence.
evidence_required: Algorithm and environment definitions, replayable workload, load/length matrix, iteration and cache telemetry, correctness and reliability data, request-level percentiles, and confidence intervals.

source_user: What assumptions must be stated before making a performance claim about continuous batching? Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer: Make the claim conditional on a defined serving workload and baseline. Record model/weights, runtime and kernel versions, hardware, precision, prompt and output lengths, arrival rate, concurrency cap, scheduler/admission rules, KV-cache capacity and paging, and the definitions of TTFT, inter-token latency, tail latency, throughput, and goodput. The mechanism is iteration-boundary retirement and admission, which can reduce idle capacity caused by different completion lengths. A boundary condition is resource pressure or low demand: queueing, synchronization, cache exhaustion, rejected requests, or OOM can erase the gain, while a homogeneous low-concurrency workload may have no idle slots to recover. Use matched requests and correctness checks; measure per-request latency, queue time, throughput/goodput, utilization, memory, cache events, and failures across load and length sweeps with repeated trials. Do not generalize beyond tested conditions.
risks: Reporting only successful requests or mean throughput can hide capacity and reliability regressions.
Claims may be overgeneralized across runtimes, schedulers, and workloads.
evidence_required: Versioned environment and baseline definitions, controlled workload traces, scheduler/cache telemetry, request-level latency and goodput, correctness, failure/rejection data, and uncertainty across tested regimes.
